title: Lead, kindly light
hook: John Henry Newman, stuck on a windless sea, writes a poem that asks for one step at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday: Father Zosima, who taught that each of us answers for everyone. Your line was responsible for all.

No wind. A sailing boat sits on flat water between Corsica and Sardinia, going nowhere. On board is an English clergyman named John Henry Newman, weak from a fever he caught in Sicily, aching to get home, and unable to move. You can't argue with a calm sea, and you can't row a sailing boat home. You can only wait. So, by the story Newman himself told, he writes a short poem. It's honest about the dark, and it asks for surprisingly little. Later it became a hymn. Today's word is its first word, and it's a request.
screen: `A SICK MAN WANTS TO GO HOME.`

segments.voice: The poem opens: "Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom, Lead Thou me on!" He doesn't ask for the wind, or a map. Then the line the poem leans on: "Keep Thou my feet; I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me." Turn it one way, and it's a confession, from the next verse: "I loved to choose and see my path; but now Lead Thou me on!" A man who liked to plan, stuck on a sea that won't take orders. Turn it another way, and it's very old. Newman called the poem The Pillar of the Cloud, pointing back to Exodus, where the King James Bible says "the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light." Israel in the wilderness never saw the whole route either; they followed the cloud. Turn it a third way, and it sounds like a psalm: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet." A lamp at night lights the ground right in front of you, and almost nothing beyond. Enough to walk. And a fourth way: his own life. The path Newman couldn't see took him somewhere he never planned. Years later he left the Church of England and became a Catholic, which cost him friends, and the Catholic Church later named him a saint. Anglicans and Catholics both claim parts of his story. The poem stays the same: one step, then the next.
screen: `I LOVED TO CHOOSE AND SEE MY PATH.`
then, large: `ONE STEP ENOUGH FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Set down the worries about how things turn out, next month, next year, the end of the road, one at a time, like heavy bags: the distant scene. Then look only at the next hour and what it asks, maybe something small: a glass of water, a reply, a rest. If you pray, borrow Newman's words, lead Thou me on; if not, let that small thing be enough.
Lead. The first word of Newman's poem, a request from someone who can't see the way: go ahead of me, and I'll follow.
Your line: one step enough. Nobody has to see the whole road to walk it. Day nine hundred twenty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Newman's poem is sung as the hymn Lead, Kindly Light in some English-speaking churches, and Christians in hard seasons sometimes pray its lines when they can't see what comes next.

fork.reveal: by Newman's own account, he wrote the poem: "I do not ask to see the distant scene; one step enough for me." the man who loved to plan asked for less.

chat.says: Everything feels so uncertain lately. What's that Newman hymn actually asking for?
options: Not the whole map. Just to be led, one step at a time: one step enough.
For the storm to end, so he could see the whole road home clearly.
For the strength to plan every step himself and never need help.
chat.meaning: Becalmed and sick, Newman asked to be led, not to see the distant scene: one step enough for me.
